security_frame.attacker: Privileged software running on the Caliptra RISC-V core (a later firmware stage, or any code that gains execution there) able to issue MMIO reads to the AES register block over the internal AHB-lite fabric.
security_frame.precondition: An earlier, more trusted context has written a plaintext block into the AES DATA_IN registers and has not yet executed the KEY_IV_DATA_IN_CLEAR trigger. No debug state, scan mode, or physical access is required.
security_frame.input: Four 32-bit MMIO reads of DATA_IN[0..3] at offsets 0x54, 0x58, 0x5c, 0x60.
security_frame.protected_asset: The AES input plaintext block held in the write-only DATA_IN registers.
security_frame.modification: The write-only DATA_IN registers have a software read path. aes_reg_top.sv:1784/1786/1788/1790 return reg2hw.data_in[0..3].q from the read multiplexer, instead of the constant zero that this same file returns for its other write-only window.

security_feature_bypassed: DATA_IN is a write-only register window. The register block must not return its stored contents to software, so that an AES input block cannot be recovered by reading back the register file.
proof_goal: Show that the DATA_IN registers are declared write-only in both the RDL and the generated subreg instance, yet a software read returns the stored plaintext for all four words, making the whole 128-bit input block recoverable; and show that the same testbench rejects the claim once the same file's own treatment of TRIGGER, its other SwAccessWO register, whose read arm at aes_reg_top.sv:1826-1831 returns a constant zero is applied to those arms.
minimum_attack_sequence: A trusted context writes a plaintext block to DATA_IN[0..3] and starts an AES operation.

The operation consumes the block into the internal state register. The DATA_IN registers retain their contents: aes_control_fsm.sv:1013 clears only the data_in_new_q tracking flag on load, not the register data.
The attacker issues four MMIO reads of DATA_IN[0..3].
The read multiplexer returns reg2hw.data_in[i].q for each word, so the attacker reconstructs the full 128-bit input block.
Reads are non-destructive, so the block can be re-read until firmware explicitly writes the KEY_IV_DATA_IN_CLEAR trigger.
expected_evidence: aes.rdl:68 declares the DATA_IN field as 'sw = w', i.e. write-only with no software read.
aes_reg_top.sv instantiates u_data_in_0 with SwAccess(caliptra_prim_subreg_pkg::SwAccessWO), so the generated declaration agrees with the RDL.
aes_reg_top.sv:1784/1786/1788/1790 nevertheless return reg2hw.data_in[0..3].q from the read multiplexer: 4 leaking read arms.

In-file control: the file contains 8 SwAccessWO field instances, the 4 DATA_IN words and the 4 TRIGGER bits. TRIGGER's read arm at aes_reg_top.sv:1826-1831 returns a constant zero, the correct treatment for a write-only window, and no TRIGGER arm returns register contents. The same file therefore demonstrates the correct behaviour it withholds from DATA_IN.
aes_reg_top.sv carries the header 'Register Top module auto-generated by reggen' from that RDL, so the audited tree contradicts its own specification.
addr_hit[21] is a live address decode at a fixed MMIO offset (AES_DATA_IN_0_OFFSET = 0x54), so the read path is reachable rather than dead code.
caliptra_reg.h exposes CLP_AES_REG_DATA_IN_0 at 0x10011054 through CLP_AES_REG_DATA_IN_3 at 0x10011060, so the addresses are firmware-reachable.
In simulation, all four DATA_IN words return the written plaintext and the concatenation reproduces the original 128-bit block exactly.
Reading DATA_IN does not clear it, so a second read returns the same plaintext and the attacker need not win a race.

With the same file's own treatment of TRIGGER, its other SwAccessWO register, whose read arm at aes_reg_top.sv:1826-1831 returns a constant zero applied to the four DATA_IN arms in a scratch copy, the identical testbench reads 0x00000000 for every word and its leak cover counter drops to zero, while its control read still succeeds.
success_criteria: Every structural gate holds, including the in-file control that TRIGGER, an equally write-only window in the same file, returns constant zero.
The directed simulation recovers the full 128-bit block, with a nonzero cover count per word so the result cannot be vacuous.
The negative control fails on patched RTL while its control read still succeeds, establishing that the testbench discriminates rather than always passing.
The finding is anchored on the audited tree's own RDL, its own generated subreg access qualifiers, and its own in-file treatment of an equivalent register.

The residency window is stated accurately: DATA_IN is overwritten with pseudo-random data only when software writes the KEY_IV_DATA_IN_CLEAR trigger (aes_control_fsm.sv:836 in state CTRL_CLEAR_I), not automatically when the block is consumed. No claim is made that the plaintext persists after that trigger runs.

No claim is made that an external SoC agent can perform this read. The AES block sits on the internal AHB-lite fabric (caliptra_top.sv:1135-1147, CALIPTRA_SLAVE_SEL_AES), so the reachable adversary is software on the Caliptra core.
No claim is made that this bug recovers an AES key. The asset exposed is the input plaintext block.
